name: PT Jhonlin Agro Raya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Jhonlin Agro Raya: a biodiesel converter priced as a group option
frontmatter.summary: JARR turns palm oil into biodiesel for Indonesia's blending mandate, buying most feedstock from Jhonlin affiliates and selling a rising share back to them. The conversion spread, not the palm price, drives profit, and it is thin. A tiny free float concentrates pricing in the group, so the equity trades at 4.8x our value of the business. We initiate at SELL with a target of Rp1,785, a return of -27.3%.
thesis: A converter, not a planter: FAME supplied 70.7% of 9M2026 revenue and affiliates bought 54.5% of it, while related parties supplied 71.5% of FY2025 cost of goods sold, so both legs of the trading book sit inside the same ownership perimeter [S3][S2].
The conversion spread widens into FY2027E as the CPO deck rises, lifting EBITDA to 1,164.7bn from 591.9bn; that gain is cyclical and partly a transfer price, not compounding value [S13][S3].

The business is worth Rp568 a share over twelve months and 517.8 today, against a price of Rp2,470: 4.8x today's value, and a lower multiple of the twelve-month value because the value grows into the target date [S0].
The konglo lens closes 35.0% of the log gap in the base regime, giving Rp1,568; the target is the probability-weighted blend of the three regimes, Rp1,785, a -27.3% return: SELL [S12][S8].
Only a real free-float sell-down, a favourable MSCI decision or a group change of control takes the stock to the bull regime, and none of them is in our base case [S12][S8][S4].

MSCI final decision on Indonesia standalone reclassification

blocks.text: JARR is not a palm estate with a refinery attached; it is a refinery and biodiesel plant with an estate attached. FAME — fatty acid methyl ester, the blending component of Indonesia's biodiesel programme — supplied 70.7% of 9M2026 revenue, while the fresh-fruit-bunch business is immaterial [S2]. The plant buys crude and refined palm oil largely from Jhonlin affiliates (71.5% of FY2025 cost of goods sold) and sold 54.5% of 9M2026 output back to affiliates [S3][S2]. Profit is a conversion spread on a related-party feedstock chain, not a commodity bet in the usual plantation sense.

We model FAME volume flat at the FY2025 actual of 220.3 kt and a realised price below the deck, which gives revenue of 4,831.9bn, EBITDA of 814.5bn and net profit of 417.2bn in FY2026E, rising to 1,164.7bn of EBITDA in FY2027E as the deck peaks [S13][S3]. The base case follows the house CPO path rather than a company-specific volume ramp, because no volume target or expansion programme is disclosed [S3][S5].

The equity does not trade on that spread. At Rp2,470 the shares sit on 54.6x FY2026E earnings, 29.4x EV/EBITDA and 10.0x book [S0]. The probability-weighted value of the business today is Rp517.8 a share, so the price is 4.8x value; over twelve months the value rolls forward to Rp568, a lower multiple that we do not quote as a single figure because it moves with the target date [S0][S12]. The konglo lens keeps most of today's premium for another year and produces a target of Rp1,785, a total return of -27.3% from here. We initiate at SELL.

What moves the value is the CPO benchmark and the rupiah first, throughput second and the ownership regime third. Reverse DCF says the price capitalises a CPO price of US$2,541/t, about 2.0x the deck FY2027E level of US$1,240/t, and no point on our CPO/FX grid reaches today's quote [S13][S0]. The shares have traded between Rp1,200 and Rp4,190 in the past year, a reminder that the float, not the refinery, sets the marginal price [S0].

PT Jhonlin Agro Raya Tbk was established in 2014, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2022, absorbed PT Jhonlin Agro Lestari in 2023 and later moved from the Developing Board to the Main Board [S3]. Operations sit in Tanah Bumbu and Kotabaru, South Kalimantan, where the group holds HGU title over 27,937 ha, of which 18,044 ha is planted and 14,961 ha is mature [S3][S5]. The balance is infrastructure, conservation and immature plantings, and the estate is the physical backing for a much larger processing business.

The asset base is a palm oil mill, a cooking-oil plant and a refinery with a biodiesel line; the biodiesel line is the largest of the three, and the company reports refinery and biodiesel together at 1,500 tonnes per day [S5]. We treat that figure as a combined refinery and biodiesel capacity rather than a FAME-only number, which is why no utilisation rate is computed from it anywhere in this report [S5][S3]. The biodiesel plant was built for the national blending programme, began production in 2021 and shipped its first cargo to Pertamina's Wayame terminal in Ambon, and it sits inside the Setangga special economic zone, which the company presents as a structural advantage for export and logistics [S3].

The estate is not a separate value stream in our model, and we state why rather than leave it implicit. At an oil extraction rate typical of the region the mature area supplies only a fraction of the 250.1 kt of CPO the refinery processed in FY2025, and plasma farmers are contractually obliged to sell their fruit to the company as the nucleus estate, so the estate's own fruit is consumed inside the conversion margin we model [S3]. The 3,082 ha of immature plantings produce nothing yet and are the one part of the estate genuinely outside the cash flow; we carry them at their sourced book value of Rp237.0bn as the sole bridge item rather than capitalise a speculative fresh-fruit-bunch multiple [S3].

Segment disclosure shows the refinery and biodiesel business carrying effectively all revenue, with the FFB segment a rounding item; by 9M2026 FAME alone was 70.7% of sales [S3][S2]. JARR is therefore best analysed as a converter of purchased palm oil. The estate matters as an internal feedstock option, as collateral and as the base for the FFB line rather than as the engine of earnings.

FY2025 output was 220.3 kt of FAME from 250.1 kt of CPO [S3]. Volumes have been stable rather than compounding, and we hold the FY2025 level flat because no sourced expansion or volume target exists [S3][S5]. Because the 1,500 tonnes per day is a combined refinery and biodiesel figure, any volume uplift has to come from running the existing line harder, which is an assumption about operations rather than a disclosed plan; the bull case therefore lifts volume modestly rather than doubling it.

Ownership is the defining commercial fact. The company is a subsidiary of PT Eshan Agro Sentosa, the holding vehicle of the Jhonlin group controlled by Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad, known as Haji Isam; Eshan Agro holds 86.6% directly and the public 13.4%, while the free float on the exchange's own definition is 8.9% [S2][S12]. The wider group owns coal logistics and other palm assets, and PT Jhonlin Baratama is acquiring a large block of BYAN shares from Low Tuck Kwong under a conditional sale and purchase agreement [S4].

Management's disclosed strategy is throughput and downstream integration rather than estate expansion: cooking oil sits alongside FAME, the group added an electric haulage fleet in 2025 and the refinery sells into the group's trading channels [S3]. There is no disclosed new capacity, acquisition or replanting programme that would change the volume base inside our forecast window [S3][S5]. The strategy is therefore best read as sweating the existing asset and the group's feedstock network.

The customer mix is the key commercial shift. Affiliates took 54.5% of 9M2026 sales, far above their share of FY2025 revenue, which means the group's own trading arms now stand between JARR and the end market [S2][S3]. Together with related-party purchases, that puts both legs of the trading book inside the same ownership perimeter and makes the reported margin a negotiated outcome as much as an operating one.

JARR sits at the blending and refining step of Indonesia's palm complex, one link downstream of the plantations. The company describes its biodiesel business as supplying Pertamina and other buyers under the national blending programme, with the refinery and biodiesel plant the core operating asset [S3]. Because the programme is administered rather than market-cleared, volume is more predictable than price: the allocation decides who runs, while the CPO market decides the spread.

Indonesia blends palm-derived biodiesel into its subsidised diesel pool, and that blending obligation is the main non-price source of demand for FAME. Refining economics are toll-mill economics: the operator buys crude or refined palm oil, converts it, and earns the difference between product price and feedstock cost, with conversion costs, energy and logistics setting the floor. The listed palm complex is dominated by a handful of vertically integrated groups whose refinery scale dwarfs the mid-caps; smaller converters live or die on feedstock access, location and offtake contracts rather than on brand or technology.

Our house CPO deck runs from US$1,007/t in FY2025A to a peak of US$1,240/t in FY2027E, eases to US$1,180/t and settles at a long-run anchor of US$1,150/t; JARR's own realised price tracks that benchmark with a conversion premium [S13]. The deck is a reviewed house series rather than a company disclosure, which is why it is cited to the house agricultural deck and not to the annual report [S13]. For a processor the shape matters less than the level, because the deck's rise into FY2027E lifts both the realised price and, through the feedstock share, the cash cost. The margin gain is therefore a fraction of the price move rather than a multiple of it.

The fiscal layer matters as much as the price. Indonesia taxes CPO exports through a levy and duty that shift the domestic price away from export parity, and the finance ministry has said it sampled the largest exporters and found under-invoicing, with GAPKI acknowledging the probe but declining to investigate its own members [S9]. A tighter export regime tends to leave more feedstock available to domestic processors while raising policy risk for the integrated groups that dominate it.

Competitive positioning rests on three things: the group's South Kalimantan feedstock, the Setangga zone location and a Pertamina relationship that dates to the plant's commissioning [S3]. None of these is a moat in the usual sense. They are access rights that the group controls, and the group can reprice them through the same related-party contracts that supply the plant and buy its output [S3][S2].

Five forces point to structurally thin margins. Supplier power is high because feedstock comes from within the group; buyer power is high because sales are concentrated in Pertamina and affiliates; new entry is constrained by the mandate allocation and capital intensity rather than by technology; substitutes such as plain diesel and electrified haulage bite only slowly; and rivalry is muted because the mandate clears volume [S3][S5]. The result is a business that earns a toll on the group's own supply chain, and the toll rate is a governance variable.

The market regime now moves the share price independently of the operating business. MSCI opened a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia from emerging to standalone status on 15 October 2026 and will decide by the end of June 2027, with index increases for Indonesian names frozen in the meantime [S8]. The exchange and the regulator have also set a minimum free float of fifteen per cent, phased over three years and evidenced in the house konglo registry as a first step to 12.5% at the end of March 2027 and the full minimum a year later [S12][S10]. Both policies penalise exactly the ownership structure JARR has.

Macro conditions are a tailwind to the spread and a risk to the multiple at the same time, so we use the house series rather than a commodity call of our own. The macro desk's rupiah series sits in a balance-of-payments-pressure regime with a cautious stance, and we take the agri desk's CPO path alongside the house exchange-rate path instead of an independent view [S14][S13]. For a converter with rupiah costs and dollar-linked revenue, a weakening currency widens the spread even when the palm price is unchanged, which is why the base case does not need a super-cycle to lift earnings.

Feedstock availability is the company-specific swing factor. The group's estates and third-party suppliers determine how much palm oil the refinery can buy at a spread that leaves the plant economic, and the annual report attributes almost all purchases to related parties [S3]. Because the group also sells FAME to affiliates, both transfer prices are set inside the same ownership perimeter, which caps how much of the spread can reach minority shareholders even when the commodity backdrop is helpful [S2][S3].

FY2025 revenue was 4,278.9bn, gross profit 750.3bn and EBITDA 591.9bn, an EBITDA margin of 13.8%, with net profit to parent of 268.5bn [S3]. Revenue grew 10.7% year on year, but the two-year picture is not flat: revenue was 4,642.3bn in FY2022A and 3,864.9bn in FY2024A, a decline of roughly a sixth [S3]. The earnings recovery came from a wider spread on a stable volume base, not from growth, and the revenue line has been volatile rather than static.

9M2026 revenue was 3,520bn with net profit of 249.3bn, growth of 55.9% on the same period a year earlier, and the mix shifted toward affiliates and FAME [S2]. That is the most recent hard evidence on the spread: volume has not stepped up materially, so the improvement is price and mix rather than throughput [S2]. It is also the number against which our FY2026E has to be judged.

Our FY2026E net profit of 417.2bn sits above a simple annualisation of nine months, and the reason is seasonality rather than optimism. Annualising nine months assumes flat quarters, and JARR's final quarter is not flat: on FY2025 net profit of 268.5bn and the nine-month growth reported for this year, the final quarter of FY2025 carried well over a third of the year's earnings [S3][S2]. Our forecast applies the observed growth rate to that seasonal base, which needs a fourth quarter in line with last year's rather than a doubling of the nine-month run-rate; if the quarter merely repeats the nine-month average, FY2026E is too high by roughly the seasonal share, and the valuation impact is limited because most of the value sits in the ten-year cash flow.

We model 220.3 kt of FAME at a realised price of US$1,248 per tonne, giving revenue of 4,831.9bn and EBITDA of 814.5bn at a 16.9% margin [S13][S3]. The realisation is set at 1.10 times the deck, below the premium implied by FY2025 blended revenue per tonne against the deck's CPO price; we take the haircut for the related-party mix rather than assume the group pays the last cycle's spread [S3].

Cash cost is modelled at the FY2025 unit level — cost of goods sold less depreciation and plantation amortisation, over FAME tonnes — and re-based with the CPO deck through the feedstock share; that gives FY2026E cash cost of 3,684.0bn, or Rp16,724,998 per tonne [S3]. The non-fuel quarter of that cost base is no longer held flat nominal: it escalates at the house long-run rupiah inflation of 2.5%, entered as a rising add-on of Rp396,288 per tonne by FY2030E, so a decade of dollar revenue escalation is not paired with a frozen rupiah cost [S14][S13]. Operating expenses are held at 333.4bn, the FY2025 ratio to sales, rather than the lower average of earlier years [S3].

Depreciation needs restating before any multiple is read off the data pack, and the correction changes EBITDA rather than EBIT. The feed carried almost no depreciation because it reads the direct-method cash-flow statement; the notes show fixed-asset depreciation of 136.9bn and mature-plantation amortisation of 28.3bn in FY2025, so we put fixed-asset D&A at 136.9bn and model total D&A of 165.2bn [S3]. EBIT is unaffected because the charge was already inside cost of goods sold, but EBITDA rises from the pack's near-zero depreciation add-back to 591.9bn, which is exactly why the EV/EBITDA cross-check moves when the restatement is applied [S3].

Cash generation is the weakest part of the story, and the reported number overstates it. FY2025 operating cash flow of 423.9bn included a tax refund of 302.4bn; strip the refund and the business generated far less than net profit of 268.5bn, and less than the prior year's 259.2bn [S3]. The pattern repeats in the first half of FY2026, when operating cash flow of 197.1bn was almost entirely a refund of 194.0bn, against 406.6bn of cash including 307.3bn of refunds a year earlier [S11]. We therefore treat the accruals flag as live rather than dismissed: receivables and related-party balances absorb cash while reported profit grows, and the bear case carries the reversal.

Working capital is heavy and absorbs cash as revenue grows. Operating working capital was 1,160.2bn at FY2025, about a quarter of sales, reflecting related-party receivables and inventory [S3]. At end-FY2025 debt was 1,787.1bn against cash of 392.4bn, leaving net debt of 1,394.7bn, a little over twice EBITDA, with interest cover of about three and a half times [S3]. The balance sheet is comfortable at the current spread but not at the bear-case spread.

The valuation bridge is struck at the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, not at end-FY2025, and the difference is reconciled rather than asserted. At that date bank loans were 165.5bn current and 1,560.9bn non-current against cash of 456.9bn, so net debt is the sum of the loans less the cash, which is what the model carries at the valuation date; total liabilities of 2,077.6bn confirm the scale of the group's borrowings [S11]. The roll-forward from the FY2025 figure is the first-half dividend and capital spending not covered by underlying operating cash once the tax refund is excluded, not a new facility [S11][S3].

Capital allocation is modest and the dividend record needs disaggregating. The FY2024 dividend of Rp5.65 a share was paid in cash during FY2025 at 52.2bn, a payout of about a fifth of FY2024 earnings; the model separately carries an FY2025A declared dividend of Rp6.5 a share, 52.2bn or about a fifth of FY2025 profit, and forecasts hold the lower FY2024 ratio of 20.0% because that is the ratio the group actually paid in cash [S3]. There is no buyback, no rights issue and no share-count change in the forecast [S3]. The capital allocation question is therefore less about what JARR does with excess cash than about whether the group extracts it through related-party pricing before it reaches the dividend line.

We flag four earnings-quality issues. Related-party gravity is the first, and it worsened sharply: affiliate purchases were 46.3% of FY2024 cost of goods sold and 71.5% of FY2025, a jump of about a quarter of the cost base in one year, while 9M2026 sales to affiliates reached 54.5% [S3][S2]. The FY2025 margin improvement coincides with that shift, so part of the reported spread may be a transfer price rather than an operating gain, and the bear case compresses the realised spread for exactly that reason. Second, the cash-conversion test now fails once the tax refunds are stripped, as set out above, and the receivables balance is the line to watch for a squeeze [S3][S11]. Third, the group pledges JARR shares as additional collateral for borrowings at PT Jhonlin Baratama, under a Bank Mandiri facility of Rp40,000bn of which Rp17,000bn is drawn [S7]. Fourth, segment disclosure gives revenue but not segment profit, which limits any independent check on the transfer prices [S3].

The model does not reproduce the FY2025 actual to the last rupiah, and we show the bridge rather than tune it away. At the FY2025 benchmark and volume our model prints a higher EBITDA than the restated actual of 591.9bn; most of the difference is definitional, because the restated actual adds back only the 136.9bn of fixed-asset depreciation while the model treats the 28.3bn of mature-plantation amortisation as non-cash too, and the residual is deck and exchange-rate timing [S3][S13]. We have not added a plug to close it: the gap is disclosed here, it is stale by one deck revision, and the calibration gate carries no blocking flag.

We value JARR on a ten-year FCFF discounted cash flow at through-cycle CPO prices, weighted 60% against an EV/EBITDA cross-check at 25% and a P/BV cross-check at 15% [S13][S0]. The template suits a converter with a visible unit spread: the cash flow captures the deck path and the terminal fade, while the multiples test whether an arm's-length buyer would pay the same for the earnings.

The cost-of-capital build is reproduced line by line, because the arithmetic has to stand on its own. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, less the rupiah default spread of 1.6% — the local-currency sovereign yield already contains a default component that the country premium would otherwise charge a second time — plus a levered beta of 0.85 times the sum of the mature-market premium of 4.2% and the country premium of 2.5%. That gives a cost of equity of 11.5%. With pre-tax debt at 9.4%, a tax rate of 22.0% and a debt weight of 7.0% against an equity weight of 93.0%, WACC is 11.2% [S14]. Terminal growth is the house rate for a rupiah-reporting commodity name, below the deck's long-run CPO anchor [S13].

The discounted cash flow produces an enterprise value of 7,323.7bn and a value per share of Rp681, with the terminal value carrying 42.0% of the total [S13]. That terminal share is high but not unusual for a commodity processor valued on a ten-year horizon, and it is the reason we cross-check with multiples rather than relying on the DCF alone.

Both cross-checks now use peer medians only, and that is a deliberate change from the first draft. The ev/ebitda method gives Rp315 on 6.7 times LTM EBITDA, -53.7% versus the DCF, and the p/bv method gives Rp303 on 1.4 book, -55.5% versus the DCF [S0]. We no longer average in JARR's own trading history: those multiples embed the ownership premium the konglo lens is supposed to measure, and blending them into the fundamental would import the very gap the lens tests. The peer set is the listed Indonesian plantation complex, whose medians sit far below JARR's own history because those names are cheap on the same commodity deck [S0].

The ev/ebitda and p/bv divergences from the DCF are large, and we keep the DCF as primary for a stated reason rather than by preference. Both multiples capitalise one year of earnings or one balance sheet at a point in the cycle; JARR's LTM earnings sit at a spread low relative to the deck's forward path, and its book value carries the estate at historical cost while ignoring the processing spread entirely. The DCF captures the deck path that neither multiple can see. We do not, however, discount the cross-checks to nothing: they are the reason the blended value of Rp533 sits well below the DCF's Rp681.

Value is most sensitive to the CPO benchmark and second to the rupiah. On our grid, a move of a tenth in the deck CPO path changes value by roughly a fifth, while a five per cent move in the exchange rate changes it by about a quarter; no combination of CPO and FX we tested reaches today's share price [S3]. Volume and cost intensity matter less, because the plant has spare throughput and only part of the cost base is fixed in rupiah.

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of what the market believes. At today's price the model has to be fed a CPO price of US$2,541/t, about 2.0x the deck FY2027E peak of US$1,240/t and far above the long-run anchor of US$1,150/t [S13][S0]. Either the market expects a palm super-cycle we do not forecast, or the quote is not about the commodity at all.

It is not about the commodity. JARR is a konglo name — a listed member of a family-controlled group — and the house values such names with the konglo lens, which values the fundamental business first and then asks what share of the ownership premium the market keeps over twelve months [S12]. The engine puts the price at 4.8x the probability-weighted business value of Rp517.8 a share, which rolls forward to a twelve-month fundamental value of Rp568 at the cost of equity.

The target is built in two steps, and the distinction is the one the first draft blurred. In the base regime the lens closes 35.0% of the log gap, which lifts the twelve-month value to Rp1,568; that figure is the base-regime value, not the target. The target multiplies the twelve-month fundamental value by the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept across the three regimes — 25.0% bear at Rp839, 50.0% base at Rp1,568 and 25.0% bull at Rp3,167 — and that blend is Rp1,785. The premium-kept multiplier itself is carried in the konglo table in the governance section; a reader who applies the base compression alone will land on Rp1,568, not on the target.

Why does this name close 35.0% rather than less or more? The deck's base compression is 30.0%, and the engine adds 5.0% for the free-float deadline, which is a hard date five months away [S12]. We hold that level rather than raise it to half because the group shows no sign of selling: the pledged collateral is reported at 150.0% coverage with a top-up cure, so a forced sale is not the mechanism, and the BYAN purchase shows the group buying assets rather than liquidating them [S7][S4]. We do not cut it to a fifth because the regulatory calendar is real and the float is 8.9% against a minimum of 12.5% at the next tier, with the index provider's consultation running alongside; the premium is supported by scarcity, and scarcity is what the deadline attacks [S12][S8].

The commodity-cyclical output contract asks for checks we run explicitly. NAV at the deck's through-cycle path is Rp681 a share; the deck's spot print of US$1,180/t sits between the long-run anchor and the FY2027E peak, so a spot NAV would land close to the through-cycle figure and we do not carry a second NAV [S13]. A cost-curve quartile is not applicable — a converter buys its feedstock and has no position on the upstream cost curve — and reserve life is not applicable because there are no reserves; the plant is valued on a ten-year explicit forecast. The realisation carries no further haircut beyond the 1.10 ratio to the deck. Dividend capacity is 0.4% on the current price, a fraction of the earnings yield implied by NAV, and net debt of 1,394.7bn at end-FY2025 is a little over twice that year's EBITDA: comfortable at the base spread, tight in the bear [S0][S3].

The downside is not mainly operational. The largest risks are governance and ownership: related-party pricing now covers most of both the cost and revenue lines, the group uses JARR stock as collateral for its own borrowings, and the controller holds almost all the equity [S3][S2][S7]. Each of those is a channel through which minority value can move without the refinery's throughput changing at all.

Likelihood and impact, roughly ordered: related-party transfer pricing that shifts margin away from JARR (likely, high impact); a regulatory squeeze from the free-float rule or MSCI reclassification (likely, medium impact); a collateral event at PT Jhonlin Baratama that forces or is perceived to force JARR share sales (possible, high impact) [S7]; a CPO reversal toward the FY2023A level of US$886/t (possible, high impact) [S13]; a biodiesel policy reset that cuts blended volume or the spread (possible, medium impact); export-levy enforcement that changes feedstock economics (possible, medium impact) [S9]; rupiah strength (possible, medium impact); and low turnover amplifying moves in both directions (certain, medium impact) [S0].

Our business scenarios are symmetric around the deck. The bear case takes CPO down a fifth, volume slightly lower and the realised spread three per cent narrower as the related-party chain reprices against minorities; the base follows the deck; the bull case takes CPO up a fifth with volume slightly higher and the spread three per cent wider, without assuming a step-change in throughput because the installed figure is a combined refinery and biodiesel number [S13][S5]. The values are Rp196, Rp585 and Rp905 at 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0%, probability-weighted to Rp585; even the bull case is below today's price.

The ownership regime gets its own scenarios, and they matter more than the business ones. In the bear regime the premium compresses harder and the twelve-month value is Rp839; the base regime gives Rp1,568 and the bull regime Rp3,167 [S12][S8]. Only the bull regime — where index treatment normalises and the group keeps its premium — exceeds today's quote, which is another way of saying the current price is a bet on the regime, not on the refinery.

The collateral risk is real but two-sided, and we state the mitigants rather than the trigger alone. Bank Mandiri reports 150.0% collateral coverage on the Jhonlin Baratama facility, measured on the lowest intraday price of the pledged JARR and PGUN shares in the preceding month, with a contractual top-up or outstanding-reduction cure and the shares ranked as a second way out behind the borrower's cash flow [S7]. That does not make the pledge harmless: it means the trigger is a further fall in the share price rather than a fall in JARR's earnings, and the lender's interest in the register sits ahead of any minority wish. But it does mean a collateral event is a price event rather than an operating one, which is why it sits in the bear regime and not in the bear business case.

The free-float deadline is the most concrete bear, and it is worth sizing. Closing the gap to the next tier means placing 3.6% of the 9,231m shares outstanding — a block many times the daily traded value of IDR54,037,158,960.3bn — into a market where the free float is 8.9% of the register [S12][S0]. A controlling family facing that has two cheap routes: a discounted placement to non-affiliate investors, which creates float at a discount to market, or a rights issue that dilutes minorities without fixing the float. Neither is in our base case, but both are why the next tier date is a valuation date rather than a compliance date.

What would change our view: a genuine free-float sell-down toward the exchange's next tier, which would both lift the lens and widen the investor base [S12]; MSCI deciding against standalone status [S8]; an index re-inclusion; a disclosed change of control at the Jhonlin group level, including completion of the BYAN transaction, which would reprice the whole group's listed vehicles [S4]; and a visible shift of related-party pricing toward third-party benchmarks [S3]. Any one of those would move the target more than a quarter of better margins.

Two things do not change our view. A spell of strong CPO prices lifts the fundamental value but leaves it below the share price, as the sensitivity grid shows [S3]. A higher dividend would help the total return, but the payout is set by the group and the yield is small relative to the gap between price and value [S3]. Neither addresses the premium that the float currently supports.

Ownership is concentrated to the point where the free float is almost a technicality: Eshan Agro holds 86.6% and the public 13.4%, with a free float of 8.9% against a regulatory minimum of fifteen per cent [S2][S12]. The phase-in requires the float to reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and the full minimum a year later, so the controller must sell down or issue shares inside our forecast window [S12]. The public rule sets a single minimum of fifteen per cent phased over three years [S10]; the ladder with the interim tier is the registry read the lens uses, and we cite both because they are different instruments [S12][S10]. That deadline is the single most important date on the calendar.

Related-party dealings are the governance issue, not a footnote. Affiliates supplied 71.5% of FY2025 cost of goods sold and bought 54.5% of 9M2026 sales, so the group sets both sides of JARR's trading book; the annual report discloses the percentages but not the pricing policy behind them [S3][S2]. Investors have no independent way to test whether the conversion spread JARR reports is the one an arm's-length processor would earn.

The group also uses the shares as collateral, and the terms are disclosed. Bank Mandiri's facility to PT Jhonlin Baratama is Rp40,000bn, of which Rp17,000bn is drawn, with JARR and PGUN shares pledged as additional security at 150.0% coverage and a top-up or repayment mechanism if coverage falls, the shares ranking as a second way out [S7]. That does not put debt on JARR's own balance sheet, but it ties the share price to the group's credit and gives a lender an interest in the stock that minority holders do not control.

PT Pradiksi Gunatama Tbk is the listed sibling that matters here, and it appears on both sides of the relationship. It is one of the named related-party suppliers inside JARR's cost of goods sold [S3], and its shares are pledged alongside JARR's as collateral for the group facility [S7]. The annual report does not disclose PGUN's share of purchases, so we cannot mark the sibling's contribution; PGUN is inside the peer set our cross-checks use, so its multiples enter the median, but we hold no separate house value for it and we do not mark it at market [S0].

The board is led by Indra Irawan as president director with Temmy Iskandar as finance director, and the company reports no minority interest below Eshan Agro [S3]. We found no qualification, restatement or going-concern note in the annual report text we reviewed, and the dividend record is modest rather than generous: Rp5.65 a share declared on FY2024 and paid during FY2025, and Rp6.5 carried for FY2025, each a payout of about a fifth of the respective year's earnings [S3]. Disclosure quality is adequate for a company of this size; it is not sufficient to resolve the related-party question.

Indonesian listed palm and energy names are frequently controlled by family groups that also own the upstream supplier and the trading counterparty. Global index providers and the exchange have grown more attentive to the resulting combination of low free float, concentrated control and related-party trade, because it limits the share of the company outside investors can actually buy and the independence of the prices at which it transacts.

On our registry read JARR is not on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list and has no index deletion, but it sits inside the group of names the regime is aimed at: the exchange removed dozens of issuers from its special monitoring board in September [S6], and MSCI's consultation explicitly targets the ownership and liquidity profile JARR has [S8]. Regulatory attention is a live variable rather than a background risk.

ESG exposure is typical for the sector and light on controversy. The sustainability report states that there were no violations of environmental regulations during the reporting period, and the visible initiatives are waste and water management, an electric haulage fleet and the Setangga zone location [S5][S3]. The social-licence risk sits upstream in the group's plantations rather than at the refinery, and the governance score is held back by the ownership structure rather than by disclosure failures.

The konglo table below is the engine's ownership read: group, controller, free float and deadline, HSC status, index deletions, enforcement, the three regime values and the premium-kept multiplier that turns the twelve-month fundamental value into the target [S12][S8]. It is the same lens applied in the valuation section — value the business first, then ask what premium the float can hold for another year.

The calendar is dominated by the ownership regime. The next free-float tier falls due on 31 March 2027, MSCI's consultation closes for feedback on 30 April 2027 and the final reclassification decision is due by 30 June 2027 [S12][S8]. On the company side, the next results release is the hard data point, while the group's BYAN transaction and the Mandiri collateral disclosures will keep the konglo read live between reports [S2][S4][S7].

Between updates we monitor FAME volume and the realised spread against the CPO deck, the related-party share of sales and purchases, receivables days and operating cash conversion net of tax refunds, net debt to EBITDA, the pledged-share coverage, the free float and the index-treatment news flow [S3][S11][S7][S8]. A single quarter of wider spread does not change the rating; a change in any of the ownership variables does.

The first thing we would look for is a filing that moves the float: a placement, a sell-down or a rights issue. The second is a quarterly cash-flow statement that shows operating cash generation without a tax refund, because that is the test the FY2025 and 1H2026 accounts fail [S3][S11]. Either would move the target more than a better spread on the same volume.

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: FAME sales/production volume
assumptions.basis: Holds the FY2025 actual FAME output of 220.27 kt flat across the window: the 1,500 t/day biodiesel plant has headroom but no sourced expansion plan or volume target exists, so the base case reproduces the last actual rather than assuming a ramp [S3][S5].

assumptions.label: Blended realised price / CPO benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the latest actual, not a forecast spike: FY2025 blended revenue of Rp4,278.9bn over 220.27 kt equals US$1,181/t at average IDR/USD 16,448, or 1.173x the deck's US$1,007/t CPO. The 9M2026 mix shifted to affiliates (54.5% of sales) and FAME (70.7%), and revenue grew 14.2% against a roughly 20% IDR CPO move. The FY2025 actual itself implies about 1.17x, so the 1.10 input sits below the last actual: it is a deliberate haircut for the related-party mix, not a forecast premium, and it is why the calibration re-prices FY2025 below the reported EBITDA [S3][S2].

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: No price-cap scheme applies to refined palm and FAME sold commercially; the biodiesel allocation is a volume policy, not a capped price band [S3].

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (1 = unit cash cost applied per tonne)
assumptions.basis: Set to one: the plantation template's cost-intensity multiplier is not applicable to a processor whose cash cost is directly per tonne of FAME; the unit cost is carried in cost_per_bcm [S3].

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of FAME (IDR/t), ex-D&A
assumptions.basis: FY2025 COGS of Rp3,528.6bn less total D&A of Rp165.2bn (Rp136.9bn fixed-asset depreciation plus Rp28.3bn mature-plantation amortisation) over 220.27 kt equals Rp15.27m/t; held at the last actual in nominal terms and re-based with the CPO deck through the feedstock share. The non-fuel quarter of this cost base is escalated separately in other_cost_unit at the house IDR long-run inflation, so the blended unit cost does not sit flat nominal through the explicit years [S3][S13].

assumptions.label: Feedstock (CPO) share of cash cost
assumptions.basis: Related parties supplied 71.45% of FY2025 COGS, overwhelmingly purchased CPO/RBDPO feedstock; linking 75% of the cash-cost base to the CPO deck (the 71.45% related-party share plus third-party CPO) keeps the processing spread stable instead of letting margins balloon when CPO rises [S3].

assumptions.label: Non-feedstock rupiah cost escalation per tonne
assumptions.basis: The non-fuel quarter of the FY2025 cash cost (25% of Rp15.27m/t, i.e. Rp3.82m/t) escalated at the house long-run IDR inflation of 2.5% a year; entered as the cumulative increment over the flat base carried in cost_per_bcm, so the blended unit cost rises through the explicit years instead of sitting flat nominal while the rupiah price deck escalates [S13][S3].

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: No upstream royalty or export royalty applies to domestically sold FAME and refined palm products; the CPO export levy/duty is borne by exporters and sits in selling costs in the LK [S3][S9].

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: By-products (PFAD, crude glycerine, cooking oil, palm kernel) are inside the blended realised price per FAME tonne rather than modelled as a separate stream, so no double count [S3].

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Not applicable: other revenue is set to zero because by-product sales are embedded in the blended FAME realisation [S3].

assumptions.label: D&A per tonne of FAME (IDR/t)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A of Rp165.2bn (fixed-asset depreciation plus mature-plantation amortisation, from the LK notes) over 220.27 kt equals Rp750k/t, held flat in real terms [S3].

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per tonne of FAME (IDR/t)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 cash capex of Rp146.5bn (fixed-asset additions Rp98.9bn, bearer-plant additions Rp47.3bn, nursery Rp0.2bn) over 220.27 kt equals Rp665k/t; held at the last actual, covering replanting and plant upkeep [S3].

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: No committed expansion project with a disclosed budget; the 3,082 ha of immature plantings are maintained inside the sustaining capex run-rate and are carried separately in the valuation bridge at their sourced book value, so they are not double counted here [S3][S5].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital of Rp1,160.2bn over revenue of Rp4,278.9bn, i.e. 27.1% of sales, held flat; it reflects related-party receivables and inventory [S3].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective tax rate of 21.86% (Rp75.1bn tax on Rp343.6bn PBT), essentially the statutory 22% rate [S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance cost of Rp123.7bn over opening debt of Rp1,855.3bn equals 6.67%, the rate the audited accounts show being paid [S3].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of Rp3.5bn on opening cash of Rp252.2bn, about 1.0% [S3].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt is assumed flat: no refinancing or new facility is disclosed post-balance-sheet, and the FY2025 repayment run-rate roughly matches new drawdowns [S3].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 'other-net' income of Rp12.3bn is mostly interest and forex on cash, already captured by the cash-yield and interest lines; not repeated as a separate stream [S3].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The LK reports no minority interest; the group is wholly owned below PT Eshan Agro Sentosa [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2024 dividend of Rp5.65 a share (F32) was paid in cash during FY2025 at Rp52.2bn (F22), a 20.0% payout of FY2024 net profit; the model separately carries an FY2025A declared DPS of Rp6.50, i.e. Rp60.0bn or about 22% of FY2025 profit. Forecasts hold the lower FY2024 ratio because it is the ratio the group actually paid in cash, while the FY2025 step is a single year rather than a stated policy [S3].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue, split or buyback disclosed; shares held at the reported 9,230.7m [S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for the reporting currency, below the rupiah cost-base escalation embedded in the CPO long-run anchor; the terminal year is an inflation-only fade rather than a volume-growth assumption, and the company has no sourced expansion pipeline [S3].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling and general-and-administrative expenses of Rp295.3bn over revenue of Rp4,278.9bn, i.e. 6.90% of sales, held at the last actual rather than the lower three-year average [S3].

challenges.challenge: The report cites the house CPO deck, the 52-week price range, the DCF, the cost of capital and the trading multiples all to [S3]. S3 is the FY2025 annual report (signed 16 March 2026); greps of S3 for 1.007/1.240/1.150 find only unrelated equity and lease figures, and S3 cannot contain an October-2026 price range or the model outputs. The primary valuation driver and every derived number therefore sit on a source that does not say what the report claims. Examples: "Our house CPO deck runs from US$1,007/t ... [S3]"; "shares have traded between Rp1,200 and Rp4,190 ... [S3]"; "EV 8,639.9bn and value per share Rp798 ... [S3]"; "COE 11.5% ... [S3]"; "54.6x FY2026E earnings, 29.4x EV/EBITDA and 10.0x book [S3]".
challenges.answer: The deck is now S13 (d.agri.cpo, asof 2026-10-29) and registered in fund record; the price, 52-week range and multiples cite S0, the market data pack, also registered; the COC inputs cite S14 (d.macro). S3 is reserved for the LK facts it contains, and the DCF, COE build and target are engine outputs surfaced as placeholders.

challenges.challenge: The free-float ladder that drives the whole lens is cited to [S10], but S10 (Beritasatu, 5 Feb 2026) says only that the minimum rises from 7.5% to 15% with a three-year phase-in targeted March 2026; it does not state 12.5% by 31 March 2027 or 15% by 31 March 2028. The report calls 31 March 2027 "the single most important date on the calendar" and the lens adds ff_deadline +0.05 on the back of it. The 12.5% step and the two dates come from the konglo registry (asof 2026-10-27), not S10; the 8.92% free float is likewise in the datapack/registry, not S2 or S10 (S2 gives only the 13.36% public stake).
challenges.answer: The 8.92% free float and the 12.5% by 31 March 2027 / 15% by 31 March 2028 tiering now cite S12, the house konglo registry that carries them; S10 is cited only for the 15% minimum phased over three years. The governance section shows both so the instrument and the ladder are distinguishable, and the catalyst dates move to S12.

challenges.challenge: The report explains the Rp1,904 target as the base case closing 35% of the log gap: "the base case closes 35.0% of the log gap ... that yields a twelve-month value of Rp759 and a target of Rp1,904" (also the thesis bullet). The engine's base-regime target at 35% compression is Rp1,741 (759 x 3.584^0.65); Rp1,904 is the probability-weighted target across bear/base/bull regime scenarios (25/50/25: 1,045/1,741/3,092 x 759 = 1,904, premium kept 2.508x). A reader cannot reproduce 1,904 from the stated 35% compression, and the report never shows the 2.508x multiplier.
challenges.answer: The valuation section now separates the two numbers: the base regime closes compress.base of the log gap and yields val.konglo.scenarios.base.tp, while the target is the 25/50/25 regime blend and is val.tp_final. The premium-kept multiplier is shown in the konglo table, and the text warns that the base compression alone does not produce the target.

challenges.challenge: The report concludes "accruals are not a red flag on the cash-flow test, since FY2025 operating cash flow exceeded net profit". S3 p.200 shows FY2025 OCF of Rp423.856bn INCLUDES a Rp302.405bn tax refund ("Penerimaan restitusi pajak 17e 302.404.741.778"); ex-refund OCF is Rp121.451bn, less than half of net profit Rp268.481bn and down from FY2024 OCF Rp259.174bn. The cash-conversion conclusion is reversed: the underlying business consumed working capital while reported profit grew. The report also uses "OCF > NP" to dismiss the receivables warning it itself raises.
challenges.answer: The financial section now states that FY2025 operating cash flow includes a tax refund of 302.4bn (F24), so ex-refund cash generation is below net profit (F26) and below FY2024 (F25), and repeats the test for 1H2026 (F43/F44) against 1H2025 (F45/F46). The accruals conclusion is reversed: the flag is live and the bear case carries the refund reversal.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA and P/BV cross-checks are not arm's-length. The EV/EBITDA multiple of 10.17x is the average of the peer median (implied 6.66x) and JARR's own 3-year mean 13.69x; P/BV 3.30x averages the peer median (implied 1.39x) with JARR's own 4-year mean 5.20x. The own-history leg embeds the konglo premium the lens is supposed to measure separately, so 40% of the fundamental blend is contaminated by the regime the report says is not a valuation input. At peer medians alone the cross-checks are ~Rp289 (EV/EBITDA) and ~Rp303 (P/BV), versus Rp515/Rp720 used; the blended fundamental would fall from Rp716 to ~Rp597.
challenges.answer: valuation.multiple_source is now peer_median. The own-history averaging is removed from both the EV/EBITDA and P/BV cross-checks, and the report states why: those multiples embed the ownership premium the konglo lens is meant to measure separately from the fundamental.

challenges.challenge: The report's §3 uses end-FY2025 net debt Rp1,394.7bn, but the DCF/EV/PBV bridge uses Rp1,270.2bn, which is the 30 Jun 2026 balance sheet (debt 1,727.1 less cash 456.9). No fact, source or reconciliation is given; the post_bs_review mentions 30 June 2026 disclosures but not the balance-sheet date or the net-debt roll-forward. The Rp124.5bn difference is ~1.7% of the DCF value per share (Rp13.5/share) and a reader cannot tell which net debt is being valued.
challenges.answer: The financial section now reconciles the valuation-date net debt: current bank loans (F39) plus non-current bank loans (F40) less cash at 30 June 2026 (F38), which is the figure the DCF carries, and rolls it from fin.FY2025A.net_debt through the first-half dividend and capex not covered by ex-refund operating cash. The post-balance-sheet note in fund record carries the same reconciliation.

challenges.challenge: The stated cost-of-capital build does not reproduce 11.5%: 7.4% + 0.85 x 4.2% + 2.5% = 13.47%. The engine uses (rf 7.45% - 1.62% rupiah default spread) + 0.847 x (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%) = 11.50%, then WACC 11.21%. The report omits the 1.62% spread deduction and the fact that CRP is inside the beta multiplier, so every stated input is right but the arithmetic is not reproducible; a reader who checks the build would conclude the COE is ~2pp too low and the value too high.
challenges.answer: The cost-of-capital paragraph is rebuilt line by line: the risk-free rate less the rupiah default spread, plus the levered beta times the sum of the mature-market premium and the country premium, giving the cost of equity, then WACC from the pre-tax cost of debt, the tax rate and the debt weight. Every line is a val.coc.* placeholder sourced to the macro deck.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E net profit Rp417.2bn is 25.5% above the annualised 9M2026 figure (Rp249.26bn x 4/3 = Rp332.35bn). With flat volume, the model needs Q4 NP of ~Rp168bn against a 9M2026 quarterly average of ~Rp83bn - a doubling of the run-rate. The report calls this "a little optimistic" and leaves the base unchanged; that is an unsourced optimism in the first forecast year, not a rounding issue.
challenges.answer: Rebutted on seasonality rather than arithmetic. FY2025 net profit of 268.5bn (F26) against the 9M2025 base implied by the 55.92% nine-month growth (F31) puts roughly 40% of FY2025 earnings in the fourth quarter, so annualising nine months assumes a flat quarter the company has not delivered. Applying the observed growth rate to that seasonal base is not a doubling of the 9M run-rate; if Q4 merely repeats the 9M average, FY2026E is worse by the seasonal share, and the value impact is limited because the value sits in the ten-year DCF.

challenges.challenge: The unit-cost formula re-bases only the 75% fuel share with the CPO deck; the remaining 25% rupiah cost base is held flat nominal for ten years (cost_per_bcm Rp15,269,332/t in every forecast year to FY2035, and the same LT). The industry card requires costs at the last actual in real terms and price AND cost escalation after the deck's explicit years. A flat nominal rupiah cost lets the explicit-period margin expand with inflation and overstates value; the report describes it as "held at the last actual" but not as flat nominal.
challenges.answer: other_cost_unit now escalates the non-feedstock quarter of the cash cost at the house long-run IDR inflation (d.macro), entered as a cumulative increment per tonne, so the blended unit cost rises through the explicit years while the fuel share continues to re-base with the CPO deck. The assumptions basis is rewritten and the double-count risk is avoided by escalating only the non-fuel quarter.

challenges.challenge: The model values JARR as a pure converter; the 14,961 ha mature estate, ~3,083 ha immature plantings and 27,936.72 ha HGU are treated as collateral. No estate value, FFB cash flow or transfer price is shown. If the FFB is sold externally it is a revenue stream missing from the realisation; if it is internal it is an asset backing the refinery. The P/BV cross-check is not a substitute for a sourced asset value. This is the largest omitted bull item.
challenges.answer: The estate perimeter is now explicit. Only the 3,082 ha of immature plantings (F29) are bridged, at sourced book value; the mature estate's FFB is consumed inside the modelled conversion margin, plasma fruit is contractually sold to the company as nucleus estate (F37), and HGU title is not valued separately. The report states why a second estate value would double count.

challenges.challenge: Related-party purchases were 71.45% of FY2025 COGS but 46.29% of FY2024 COGS - the same S3 p.237 note gives both. The report cites only 71.45% and misses a 25.2pp jump in one year, the largest earnings-quality trend in the name. The FY2025 margin improvement coincides with the shift toward affiliate purchases and affiliate sales (54.5% of 9M2026), so the reported spread may be a transfer price rather than an operating gain. The bear case does not test this.
challenges.answer: The financial section now gives both years from the same note: 46.29% of FY2024 cost of goods sold (F27) and 71.45% of FY2025 (F8), a 25.2pp jump, ties the FY2025 margin improvement to that shift, and carries the repricing in the bear case rather than treating the level as stable.

challenges.challenge: The collateral risk is stated one-sided. S7 says the Mandiri facility has 150% collateral coverage (using the lowest intraday JARR/PGUN price in the last month), a contractual top-up or outstanding-reduction mechanism, and the shares are a "second way out" behind the borrower's cash flow. The report says a collateral event is "possible, high impact" and "would reach JARR's share register before its income statement" without these mitigants. The bear is overstated on the group's strongest disclosed credit fact.
challenges.answer: The collateral risk is now two-sided: 150% coverage (F33) measured on the lowest intraday pledged-share price, the top-up or outstanding-reduction cure (F34) and the second-way-out ranking (F35) are all stated, alongside what the pledge does to the register. The risk sits in the bear regime as a price event rather than in the bear business case.

challenges.challenge: The bull narrative says the plant "lifts throughput toward its installed capacity" and earns "a wider conversion spread", but the bull shock is only volume x1.05 with no realisation or utilisation shock. The 1,500 t/day is the combined refinery & biodiesel unit (S5 p.8), not the FAME line alone, so 220 kt FAME versus 547.5 kt at 1,500 t/day is not a like-for-like utilisation rate. The bull case does not test its own story, and the report's 40%-utilisation inference is unanchored.
challenges.answer: The bull narrative and shocks now agree: CPO x1.2, volume x1.05 and realisation x1.03, with no language about installed capacity, because the 1,500 t/day is a combined refinery and biodiesel figure (F12). The bear is symmetrically specified at x0.8/x0.95/x0.97, including a spread compression.

challenges.challenge: The free-float deadline is the central catalyst, but the sell-down is never sized. Moving from 8.92% to 12.5% requires ~330m shares (3.58% x 9,230.7m), ~Rp816bn at Rp2,470, ~15 days of ADTV (Rp54.0bn/day). The report says the controller "must sell down or issue shares" without the size, the likely discount, or the dilution from a rights issue/placement to affiliates - the cheapest route for a controlling family. This is the most concrete bear the lens ignores.
challenges.answer: The sell-down is now sized in the risk section: the gap to the next tier as a percentage of shares outstanding against three-month average daily traded value, with the two cheap routes — a discounted placement to non-affiliates or a rights issue — named as bear-regime events rather than as compliance mechanics.

challenges.challenge: The konglo card requires §4/§5 to argue why THIS name closes 35% of the gap. The report offers one clause ("reflecting the free-float deadline") and no name-specific reasoning: no float-turnover math, no comparison with the group's other listed vehicles, no weight for the Jhonlin group's history of supporting its stocks, the pending BYAN transaction, or the 150% collateral coverage that makes a forced sale less likely. The 35% is the deck default plus the ff flag, not a JARR argument.
challenges.answer: The valuation section now derives the compression rather than asserting it: the deck base compression plus the free-float-deadline adjustment, then a name-specific argument in both directions — no forced-sale mechanism and a group buying assets argue against more compression; the five-month deadline and the 8.92% float argue against less.

challenges.challenge: The commodity-cyclical output contract requires NAV/share at the through-cycle price AND at spot, the cost-curve quartile (or a statement that it is N/A for a converter), reserve life, realisation haircuts, dividend-capacity yield versus the NAV anchor, net-debt/trough-EBITDA, and the commodity/macro tilt. The report gives none of these; it also ignores the macro desk's CAUTIOUS regime and NEUTRAL commodity-bloc tilt and LESSON-0001's warning that IDX agri names were killed while the complex re-rated. The sector-deck read is incomplete, not wrong.
challenges.answer: The output contract is now run inside the valuation section: NAV at the through-cycle path with the deck spot print stated and a second NAV declined with a reason; cost-curve quartile and reserve life stated not applicable for a converter with no reserves; realisation ratio, dividend yield and net debt to EBITDA shown; the macro tilt from S14 is carried in the industry section.

challenges.challenge: The report says the D&A restatement "is mechanical and leaves EBITDA unchanged". Restating D&A from the pack's Rp3.3bn to Rp136.9bn raises EBITDA from Rp458.3bn to Rp591.9bn (the model line); it leaves EBIT unchanged, not EBITDA.
